note: Fe's half of the Phase 0 manifest (00b-oracle-and-differential-corpus.md). kg owns the sibling test/lisp-compat/features.json (sub-plan 00C); the two id spaces must not collide, checked by utils/check_compat_manifest.py. This file intentionally holds only the handful of entries needed to prove the mechanism -- populating the corpus is 00C's job, not this one's.

features.rationale: Fe's error text already carries Emacs' condition name ('void-function <symbol>'), by design (see fe.c's HandleNonCallable/HandleVoidSymbol comments), but until Phase 6 it is prose in FeHandleError()'s message rather than a structured, catchable condition object. Every recorded Fe-side record for this feature carries condition_source: "message" for exactly that reason.

Fe has no hash-table type, no reader syntax for one, and no primitives that construct or query one. Not on this program's roadmap; the compat runner short-circuits cases naming this feature instead of running them and pattern-matching an unbound-symbol error that would look identical to a real gap.

Fe has no signal primitive and no condition hierarchy; both arrive with Phase 6 (parent plan section 6, 'Introduce structured completion and non-local control'). Until then Fe reports an ordinary void-function condition instead of the quit Emacs raises for (signal 'quit nil); this is deliberately not a required-match feature yet, so run-fe-compat.py reports the gap without failing the corpus over it.

Emacs's plain (non-cl-lib) namespace does not define `assert` at all under `emacs -Q --batch`; Fe's `assert` is a core primitive with no direct oracle analogue by this name. Recorded as divergent rather than kg-policy because the disagreement is meaningfully demonstrated by a real oracle snapshot (void-function), not merely undemonstrable.

Emacs has no `env` primitive bound in `emacs -Q --batch`; Fe's `env` is a core introspection primitive returning the interpreter's whole current symbol list (fe.c's PEnv arm), a Fe-specific capability with no Emacs analogue by this name.

Same name, incompatible shape: Emacs's `let` takes a bindings list as its first argument and signals wrong-type-argument when given a bare symbol; Fe's `let` takes a bare symbol directly and has no separate body argument at all. kg's prelude `let` macro (tracked in kg's own manifest, owner kg, comparison emacs) is the Emacs-shaped construct; this entry is Fe's distinct low-level primitive.

Return-value divergence only; the mutation itself (CAR becomes 9) is not independently observable through this case's shared single-expression protocol, but the printed return value already demonstrates the disagreement.
Return-value divergence, same root cause as primitive-setcar: fe.c's PSetCdr arm never assigns its `res` return value.

Sub-plan 05C: `>` is a new fe core primitive joining `<`/`<=` in the chained comparator loop (05A row C2). The chaining behaviour is pinned by the num-greater-chain case, which this entry shares with the row that owns it.

Sub-plan 05C: `>=` is a new fe core primitive joining the chained comparator loop (05A row C2). The chaining behaviour is pinned by the num-greater-chain case, which this entry shares with the row that owns it.

Sub-plan 05C: `/=` is a new fe core primitive, strictly binary (05A row C3) -- exact inequality across both numeric types, with the third-operand wrong-number-of-arguments enforced at dispatch. Both cases are shared with the num-not-equal row that owns them.

Phase 5, row T1: `integerp` is an fe core primitive landed by 05C, answering from the tag alone and never raising on a non-number. It is pinned by num-predicates-tags, which names only primitives fe has, so the row's status is evidence about `integerp` rather than about a case it shares. It used to name num-predicates and sit at `planned` because that case also asks about kg's `numberp`; num-predicates keeps that case and that status.

Phase 5, row T1: `floatp` is an fe core primitive landed by 05C, answering from the tag alone and never raising on a non-number. Pinned by num-predicates-tags alongside primitive-integerp, for the same reason: the shared num-predicates case also asks about kg's `numberp` and cannot flip in fe's corpus, which is a fact about that case, not about this primitive.

Zero operands is the identity element, 0, as in Emacs -- and `(-)` is 0 too, while `(/)` has no identity and stays wrong-number-of-arguments (primitive-div). Fe's arithmetic frame used to complete with the evaluator's internal `&unbound` sentinel when no operand had been combined, which escaped into Lisp and crashed `funcall`.
Zero operands is the identity element, 1, the sibling of primitive-add's own zero-operand case.

The 04D namespace cut, as recorded: the bootstrap moved into function cells and the value-cell call-position fallback was deleted, so the primitive `car`'s value cell is empty and `(boundp 'car)` is nil -- the Lisp-2 answer this snapshot has pinned since 00C. The pre-cut Fe reported t because a single value cell held both the primitive and any value of that name; the cut is what flipped the answer.

Sub-plan 04D: `#'x` now reads as `(function x)` -- Read's `#` case routes through the same ReadWrapped construction `quote` uses, with `stray '#''` kept for a bare `#'` -- and the writer prints `(function X)` as `#'X` the way Emacs' printer does, so `(quote #'car)` reads as `(quote (function car))` and prints `#'car`. The pre-cut reader treated `#'` as identity, and its own historical rationale (a stale fe.c line number in the pre-cut tree) described that gap.

Sub-plan 05D's cut: `42.0` now reads as a float and prints as `42.0` (this case's pinned answer), and `42` reads as an integer -- the reader/printer half of Phase 5's numeric split. The old one-type divergence ('42 and 42.0 are the same object and print the same') is gone: an integral float keeps its `.0` (P1), so the float never impersonates an integer on output.

Deliberately not implemented: FeReadFn (fe.h's public read callback) yields one raw byte at a time with no lookahead buffer for multi-byte reassembly at the reader's character-literal site, so `?Ã©` (a two-byte UTF-8 encoding) would read only its first byte -- exactly the silent wrongness this compat manifest exists to prevent. Failing clearly (void-variable on the resulting bare symbol) is the current, intentional behavior rather than a bug to fix; a real implementation needs the reader's byte source to support decoding a full codepoint, which is untracked.

Parent plan section 7 ('Make strict arity normal') is Phase 7, milestone 2, not yet implemented or funded by this slice's Decision. Fe's `-a`/`fe -a` strict-arity pass exists standalone (test.sh's third pass) but is opt-in, not the evaluator's default -- this entry tracks the *default* mode's behavior, which is what an ordinary `(lambda ...)` call site sees.

This is the parent plan's own example of a divergence-from-Fe that is an agreement-with-Emacs: kg's fe fork changed vanilla Fe's historical behavior (silently returning nil for an unbound symbol) specifically to match Emacs's void-variable signal, and doc/fe-upstream.md's divergence table records that as a deliberate, already-landed change, not a Phase 2+ item. Status is `supported` because the oracle comparison is what this manifest tracks; the vanilla-Fe distinction is prose context only, not a comparison axis this schema has a field for.

This is kg/fe's own deliberate policy, not an Emacs contract: the parent kg repository's CLAUDE.md already states the precedent for exactly this shape of decision (kg_regex_match_backward's backward-matching policy is kg's own, not Emacs', so an oracle for it would have to encode kg's policy rather than read Emacs'), and 00b-oracle-and-differential-corpus.md's own 'What this does not do' names cyclic-structure printing explicitly. Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts all three bounded forms (#<cycle>, #<deep>, #<truncated>).

Sub-plan 02B lands `setq` as a core special form (fe.c's EvaluateSetq, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PSetq arm): pair iteration over the existing assignment path, updating the innermost lexical binding when one exists and the global value cell otherwise. Sub-plan 02C then deleted the historical assignment `=` it landed beside, so `setq` is Fe's only assignment special form and `=` is numeric equality (primitive-numeric-eq).

Sub-plan 02B lands `set` (fe.c's EvaluateSet, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PSet arm) as an ordinary, exact-arity function using the existing global setter FeSet() -- it always writes the symbol's global value cell and never reads or changes a lexical binding of the same spelling, unlike `setq`.

Sub-plan 02C repurposes `=` as numeric equality over Fe's existing doubles (fe.c's EvaluateNumericEqual, reached from EvaluatePrimitive's PNumericEqual arm, formerly the assignment primitive PAssign/primitive-assign-eq, now deleted): a left-to-right chained comparison, at least one argument required, every argument form evaluated left to right before any value is type-checked, and every operand validated and compared without short-circuiting once the result is already known. Phase 5 later extends this to integers/mixed types without redefining it, so these cases are written to leave room for that.

Sub-plan 04C, the phase's headline: a symbol holds a value (7) and a function (an fset'd lambda) at once, call position resolves the function cell, bare-symbol evaluation the value cell, and (list f (f)) is (7 9). 04D then moved the bootstrap into function cells and deleted the value-cell fallback; this case's comparison is unchanged by the cut.

Phase 4 semantics, value namespace only: `let` binds names in the value namespace and must not shadow a function of the same spelling, so `(car (list 1 2))` still resolves the primitive. Fe's `let` primitive takes a bare symbol, so the Emacs-shaped bindings list is a separate, already-divergent shape (primitive-let); the function-cell side of the split is what this case pins. Not flippable yet, and 04E (now landed) was never the blocker: fe cannot read the Emacs-shaped bindings list this case is written in at all, because fe's own `let` takes a bare symbol. That lands when an Emacs-shaped `let` moves into fe's core -- Phase 8 Wave A of the kg plan set -- and this row flips with it.

Phase 4 primitive `funcall` (04C): it takes a *value*, here a lexical closure, so the function cell of the name is irrelevant. The funcall machinery itself is complete; what the comparison still waits on is the case's Emacs-shaped `let` bindings list, which fe's bare-symbol `let` cannot read -- not 04E, which has landed. An Emacs-shaped `let` in fe's core is Phase 8 Wave A of the kg plan set (the same blocker as lisp2-let-no-function-shadow).

Sub-plan 04C: a symbol passed to `funcall` is a designator resolved through its function cell, following the same indirection call-position lookup uses, so `(funcall 'g)` calls the fset'd lambda and returns 9. A self-referential chain dies with cyclic-function-indirection rather than exhausting the step budget.

Sub-plan 04C: `apply` spreads its final list argument into the call, so `+` is called with 1 2 3 4 and returns 10. Implemented as an evaluate-then-redispatch on the frame stack (the plan's chosen shape, see doc/implementation.md); a non-list final operand is `apply: last argument must be a proper list`.

What `funcall`/`apply` may be handed: a function, never a macro or a special form, which Emacs signals invalid-function for. Fe's evaluate-then-redispatch shape makes this a correctness requirement rather than a nicety -- the redispatched `(callable (quote v) ...)` form reaches a raw-form callable as the wrappers themselves, so `(funcall 'quote 'a)` answered `(quote a)` and `(funcall 'if 1 2 3)` chose a branch of quoted forms. The classification is read off the evaluator's own primitive routing and is exposed to hosts as the C API's FeIsFunction().

Which name a dead designator chain is reported at: the one the program wrote, not the last link the resolver reached. Emacs answers `void-function chain-head` for both `(chain-head)` and `(funcall 'chain-head)`; fe's call position always did, and its funcall arm named the tail until the resolver stopped reporting a `dead` link at all.

Phase 4 primitive `fboundp` (04C) asks the function namespace; the 04D cut moved the bootstrap into function cells, so the primitive `car`'s function cell is occupied and `(fboundp 'car)` is t, matching the 04A-pinned oracle. The pre-cut answer was nil because `car` still lived in a value cell.

Phase 4 designator rule for `functionp`: a symbol whose function cell holds a function is t, an unbound name is nil, never an error. The blocker is not 04E (landed) but that fe has no `functionp` primitive at all, so the comparison still fails on void-function functionp. Fe now exposes the predicate to its hosts as the C API's FeIsFunction() -- the designator chain, macros and special forms answered exactly as Emacs' `functionp` answers them -- and the row flips when a Lisp-callable `functionp` exists, whether fe grows the primitive or kg's native is rewritten onto FeIsFunction().

Sub-plan 04C call-position semantics, sharpened by the 04D cut: call position resolves the function cell and an empty cell is void-function -- naming the head symbol -- even when the value cell is full. Reported as FeHandleError()'s message text (the parent plan's message-level rule until Phase 6), which is how the runner matches the oracle's structured void-function condition.

Sub-plan 04C: `symbol-function` returns the function cell's object -- a designator stays a symbol -- and `funcall` calls it, so the roundtrip returns 5. The printed-closure question is avoided by comparing behaviour, per 04A's data decision.

Phase 4 primitive `symbol-value` (04C) reads the value cell directly; the explicit read of a setq'd name agrees, and the mirror arm `lisp2-symbol-value-primitive` passed once the 04D cut emptied the primitive `car`'s value cell, so `(symbol-value 'car)` signals void-variable -- the explicit-value-namespace mirror of one-namespace-boundp's nil.
Sub-plan 04C: `fmakunbound` empties only the function cell, so the subsequent call is void-function j. The pair with the two keeps-* cases pins that the unbound operations act on disjoint cells.
Sub-plan 04C cell separation: `makunbound` acts on the value cell only, leaving the function cell intact, so `(m)` still returns 2. One half of the disjointness the split must preserve.

Sub-plan 04C cell separation, mirror arm: `fmakunbound` leaves the value cell alone, so the bare symbol still evaluates to 1. Together with lisp2-makunbound-keeps-function it records that unbounding one namespace never touches the other.

Sub-plan 04C: `defalias` points one symbol's function cell at another symbol, and call-position resolution follows the designator chain, so `(first (list 1 2))` behaves like `car` and returns 1; `defalias` returns the aliased symbol (first), per the 04A snapshot.

Sub-plan 04C designator rule, timing: function-cell symbol indirection is resolved at call time, not at defalias time -- `a` is aliased to `b` before `b` gets a function, and calling `(a)` afterwards still returns 1. FeGetFunction (the host API, 04C) follows that same chain.

Sub-plan 04C: `(function (lambda ...))` is a raw-form special form producing a real closure value -- not a designator -- and `funcall` calls it directly, returning 3. Since the 04D reader change, `#'(lambda ...)` reads as this same form (reader-sharp-quote-identity). Known gap, deliberate and unsnapshotted: fe accepts only a symbol or a lambda/fn form, so `(function 5)` is `unsupported-function-form`, where Emacs' `function` is plain `quote` and answers 5. Fe rejects what it cannot make a callable out of rather than quietly handing back a non-function, and the 04A pin names that spelling; a case for it would record a divergence nobody intends to close.

Sub-plan 04C: `fset` evaluates both arguments -- the first is a value naming the target symbol, not a quote -- so the symbol named by `s` (k) receives the function and `(k)` returns 4. Sub-plan 04E has since landed: kg's prelude defines its 52 functions in the function namespace, respelled from the old `setq` forms to `defalias`, `fset`'s sibling primitive writing the same cell.

kg-policy representation divergence, recorded by Phase 4's own plan (04A): Emacs stores a macro as a (macro . FUNCTION) cons in the function cell, observable only through (symbol-function 'NAME); fe has a distinct FeTMacro type and prints a macro value as (macro PARAMS BODY). Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts '(macro (a) a)' renders '(macro (a) a)'. The Phase 4 function-cell work (04C) must not imitate the cons representation to pass a case nobody wrote yet; this is kg-policy because Emacs has no anonymous macro object to snapshot at all.

Phase 5, row R1: the numeric split exists -- `42` is an integer and `42.0` a float, the type_names[] slot (05B) fed by the integer reader (05D). The case names `type-of`, which is a kg native and not an fe primitive, so the standalone fe binary this corpus drives answers `void-function type-of`: this stays a planned target snapshot in fe's corpus, and the comparison lives in kg's manifest. Two separate things are pending, and only one of them is a gap: the missing primitive is a fact about fe's surface, while the *spelling* is a real divergence -- fe's type_names[FeTDouble] is "double" where Emacs' type-of says `float`, so even with a type-of primitive fe would answer (integer double), not (integer float). Renaming the type ripples through every `expected double, got X` message and is not funded here; the integer tag closed the integer half of this row and no more.
Phase 5, row R2, landed at 05D's cut: `1.` reads as the integer 1 (Decision 3's trailing-dot integer), and `1.5` is still a float.
Phase 5, row R3, landed at 05D's cut: a leading-dot token is a float -- `.5` reads as `0.5` (Decision 3).
Phase 5, row R4, landed at 05D's cut: a signed integer literal reads as an integer -- `+5` is the integer 5 (Decision 3).
Phase 5, row R5, landed at 05D's cut: a bare exponent makes a token a float -- `1e3` reads as `1000.0` (Decision 3).
Phase 5, row R6, landed at 05D's cut: `0x10` is a symbol, not a hex number -- strtod's hex parsing died with the classifier (Decision 3).
Phase 5, row R7, landed at 05D's cut: `inf` and `nan` are unbound symbols, not numbers -- strtod's inf/nan parsing died with the classifier (Decision 3).

Phase 5, row R7's sign rule, landed after 05D: the nonfinite exponent spellings are read only with an explicit `+`. `ClassifyExponent` originally accepted `INF`/`NaN` whenever the exponent was not *negative*, which let unsigned `1eINF`/`1eNaN`/`1EINF` through as nonfinite floats where Emacs reads symbols; the classifier now records that a `+` was seen rather than that a `-` was not.
Phase 5, row R8, landed at 05D's cut: a partial exponent token is a symbol -- `1e` reads as a symbol, the classifier deciding before any conversion (Decision 3).
Phase 5, row R9, landed at 05D's cut: `9007199254740993` reads and prints exactly -- int64 exactness past 2^53 (Decision 3's integer reader on top of 05B's object).
Phase 5, row R10, landed at 05D's cut: signed zero survives read->print as `-0.0` (Decision 4's shortest-round-trip printer, which never folds -0.0's sign).
Phase 5, row P2, landed at 05D's cut: floats print shortest-round-trip, not %.7g noise -- `0.1` prints `0.1` (Decision 4's dtoastr-style loop).
Phase 5, row P3, landed at 05D's cut: positive infinity prints `1.0e+INF` and reads back as +inf (Decision 4).
Phase 5, row P4, landed at 05D's cut: negative infinity prints `-1.0e+INF` and reads back as -inf (Decision 4).
Phase 5, row P5, landed at 05D's cut: NaN prints in the pinned Emacs spelling `-0.0e+NaN`/`0.0e+NaN` (sign bit only) and reads back (Decision 4).

Phase 5, row A1 (05C, landed): unary minus is negation -- (- 5) is the integer -5. The tower's seed path gives the single-operand reduction the Emacs answer; the pre-tower seed ignored the minus and answered 5.
Phase 5, row A2, landed at 05D's cut: unary `/` is the truncated reciprocal -- `(/ 5)` is the integer 0, reachable at last because `5` reads as an integer.
Phase 5, row A3, landed at 05D's cut: integer division truncates toward zero -- `(/ 7 2)` is 3 and `(/ -7 2)` is -3, reachable at last because the literals read as integers.
Phase 5, row A4 (05C, landed): a mixed integer/float division promotes to float -- 3.5, not 3. The tower's single promotion rule.
Phase 5, row A5, landed at 05D's cut: integer division by zero is `arith-error`, reachable at last because `1` and `0` read as integers (carried in FeHandleError()'s message until Phase 6).
Phase 5, row A6 (05C, landed): all-integer arithmetic stays integer -- (* 2 3) is the integer 6. The tower's integer-preserving combine.
Phase 5, row A7, landed at 05D's cut: mixed addition promotes to float and prints `3.0` -- the 05D printer's `.0` guarantee, on top of 05C's promotion rule.

Phase 5, row A8, the recorded divergence, now visible at 05D's cut: int64 overflow is an arith-error-style message, never a bignum (modern Emacs prints the bignum 18446744073709551616); use __builtin_*_overflow, never UB (05A Decision 5). With 05D's reader the literal operands are integers, so `(* 4611686018427387904 4)` raises `arith-error` where Emacs answers the bignum -- the divergence row 05A pinned. `expt` diverges the same way and now has its own case: `(expt 2 63)` is `arith-error` here and the bignum 9223372036854775808 in Emacs. It is pinned separately because it reaches the int64 edge through its own per-signature math native rather than through the tower's ckd_mul reduction, so a fix or a change to one does not automatically move the other.
Phase 5, row C1 (05C, landed): `<` is variadic and chained -- (t nil). The comparator loop compares every adjacent pair; the pre-tower binary arm ignored the third operand and answered (t t).
Phase 5, row C2 (05C, landed): the new comparators `>` and `>=` chain too -- (t t). Both are fe core primitives sharing the comparator loop with `<`/`<=`/`=`.

Phase 5, row C3 (05C, landed): `/=` is an fe core primitive, strictly binary -- three operands are wrong-number-of-arguments, and so is one (unlike the chained comparators, whose single-operand form is `t`), enforced at dispatch since lambda arity stays lax.
Phase 5, row C4 (05C, landed): numeric `=` is mathematical value equality across types -- 3 equals 3.0. The extended chained `=` arm.
Phase 5, row C5 (05C, landed): comparison type errors say wrong-type-argument, replacing the expected-double texts on the numeric family. 05A Decision 5.

Phase 5, row C1/C5's arity edge, landed after 05D: a single operand is `t` for `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, with no type check at all, because a chain of one has no adjacent pair to compare. fe validated that one operand up front and answered `wrong-type-argument` where Emacs answers `t`; the check is gone and the comparator loop now expresses the rule by construction. `/=` is the exception and has its own case on the num-not-equal row -- it is binary, so one operand is `wrong-number-of-arguments`.

Phase 5, rows C1/C4/C5, landed after 05D: a chained comparison stops at the first false pair, Emacs' `arithcompare_driver` rule, so `(< 2 1 "a")` and `(= 1 2 "a")` are nil and the string is never type-checked -- while `(< 1 2 "a")` and `(= 1 1 "a")`, true up to the bad operand, do reach it and are `wrong-type-argument` on both sides. Both shapes are pinned deliberately: an implementation that simply stopped type-checking the tail would satisfy the first pair of cases and fail the second. Only the check short-circuits; every operand *form* was evaluated before the comparison arm ran.

Phase 5, rows E1-E3, landed at 05D's cut: fe-core `eq` is pointer identity or both-integers-equal -- `(eq 3 3)` t, `(eq 3.0 3.0)` nil (boxed floats), `(eq "a" "a")` nil. 05E deletes kg's prelude alias of `is` in the pin commit.
Phase 5, rows E4-E5, landed at 05D's cut: fe-core `eql` is `eq` or same-type numbers equal by bits -- `(eql 3 3.0)` nil (type-strict), `(eql 0.0 -0.0)` nil (the sign bit differs).

Phase 5, row E6: the kg prelude `equal` rewrite target -- strings -> string=, numbers -> eql, else eq. Lands in 05E; standalone fe has no `equal`, so this stays a planned target snapshot in fe's corpus.
Phase 5, row M1, landed at 05D's cut: sqrt returns a float, always -- `(sqrt 16)` prints `4.0`, the 05D printer's `.0` guarantee.
Phase 5, row M2, landed at 05D's cut: expt's per-signature rule from 05C, with the float column printing `256.0` at last via the 05D printer.

Phase 5, row M3: the rounding family returns integers in the *core* build (05C's per-function return types, pinned by TestMathNatives), but this case runs against the standalone fe binary, where Fex shadows floor/ceiling/truncate with one-argument versions and (ceiling -7 2) answers -7 rather than -3. The Fex shadowing is a recorded fact 05C works around, not something to fix; the row cannot flip while the compat harness targets the Fex binary.

Phase 5, row M4: the core `round` is round-half-even (2.5 to 2, 3.5 to 4) and returns an integer (05C), but the standalone fe binary's `round` is Fex's half-away `round()` -- (round 2.5) answers 3 -- so the case cannot flip while the compat harness targets the Fex-shadowed binary.
Phase 5, row M5, landed at 05D's cut: transcendentals are floats always -- `(sin 0)` prints `0.0`, the 05D printer's `.0` guarantee.

Phase 5, row Z1: `zerop` is kg's prelude one-liner over `=` (no fe spend), and standalone fe has no `zerop` at all, so both cases answer `void-function zerop` and this stays a planned target snapshot in fe's corpus; the comparison lives in kg's manifest. The wrong-type case rides =`'s 05C error name once it is compared there. Nothing in fe can flip this row -- it is not waiting on an fe-side slice.

Phase 5, row T1: integerp/floatp land as fe core primitives in 05C (answered from the tag alone), but this case also names `numberp`, which stays kg's native (widened to two tags in 05E) and does not exist in standalone fe -- so the case cannot flip in fe's corpus until it no longer depends on a kg-owned name. Fe must never add a numberp primitive (manifest collision).

Phase 5, row A8's reader sibling (05A Decision 3): an integer literal that overflows int64 reads as a double -- the pre-bignum Emacs behaviour -- while modern Emacs reads it as a bignum. 2^64 (= 18446744073709551616) is the canonical example: Emacs prints the bignum 18446744073709551616, fe reads the nearest double and prints its shortest round-trip. The alternative -- a read error -- would punish pasted constants. The fall-back is bounded by the reader's token buffer, not by magnitude: `ReadAtom`'s `char buf[64]` caps a token at 63 characters, so a literal of 64 or more digits is `symbol too long` and never reaches the classifier at all. 2^64 is 20 digits and is well inside that; a caller who pastes a 64-digit constant gets a reader error rather than a double, and this row does not claim otherwise.
